P1.evidence: The application was acknowledged but deliberately not read back — "I've seen your application, and now I'm kind of an old-school guy and would like to hear it from you" — which is a defensible style choice but is not what P1a credits. No four-part frame, no frame agreement. The open question ran: "What is it that's brought you here, actually, and how can we help you?"

P2.evidence: Work and diet were genuinely well covered — chef hours, 30,000 steps a day, the sedentary restaurant build, tasting habits, the big meal at lunch, existing intermittent fasting. Everything else is thin or absent, and on this prospect the absences are severe. Age was volunteered; height and weight were never asked at all. Health conditions were never asked — the IBS, the ulcers, the arthritis diagnosis and the cortisone injection all arrived because the prospect offered them, which under the scoring rule is a miss even though the rep did follow up well once they landed ("So with this IBS, like, how long has it been going on?", "going on for how long?"). The injury question was never asked either: the neck and shoulder came out in the opening monologue, and while the rep probed the mechanism ("What was the accident? What happened?") he never asked what the prospect is currently restricted from doing, what his clinicians have said, or whether he is cleared to load. Sleep and energy were never touched on a man describing constant pain and fourteen stress ulcers.

P3.evidence: The deep end was reached but mostly by the prospect walking there himself. The reflect-back is clean and early — "from what I'm hearing, you're here not for the vain aesthetics, you're basically here to get stronger, to get back to your real life" — and the rep then did the one thing this phase exists for, deliberately: he picked up the fatherhood thread and pressed it. "the one thing that you said that you want to become a dad... this is playing the long-term game, the longevity game", tied to the prospect's own elderly parents, and it landed at full force: "there's no bigger why." Against that, none of the opening goal questions ran — no one-thing-you'd-change, no mobility/strength/energy menu, no what-does-that-do-for-you — and the bridge was delivered as a statement rather than asked.

P4.evidence: The best P4 in the batch. "What was always missing?" and "What was throwing you off?" produced a complete and honest failure analysis: nine months in a gym five days a week for no result, stopping when the pain crossed from soreness into real pain, hating the environment. The rep then named the mechanism precisely — "when you're attending something that deep down subconsciously you don't like, even when you perform the workout it's like mid" — and the prospect finished it: "Half in, half out." The gap was named by the prospect unprompted ("having someone to motivate me... keeping you accountable, that helps me, for sure, because if I'm just by myself, I find all the excuses"), and the P4f move arrived from his side in the form of the shoemaker proverb — "I know how to make a nutritional plan, that's no problem. But still, I'm a chef, and I cheat all the time."

P5.evidence: The only consequence frame this rep ran in five sales calls, and it worked immediately: "probably, if we would be speaking like, I don't know, two years from now, if you would be not doing anything, it would be…" → "I would be destroyed, destroyed. I would not be able to move." He followed with the should-versus-how reframe as a line-in-the-sand substitute — "you're not in a, should I do it place? You're in a, I need to do it as soon as possible" — which the prospect confirmed. The settling question and the why-not were both skipped, so the frame was landed but never sharpened.

P6.evidence: The best commitment check in the batch, and notable for confronting rather than flattering. The all-in question was asked before anything was presented and was preceded by an explicit callout of the prospect's own history: "there's one like yellow flag over here when you say that you haven't been consistent, that you have a lot of excuses... this is going to suck probably, especially in the beginning... are you willing to embrace that suck and push through?" It produced a long, specific, self-aware answer. The belief question then ran verbatim before the price: "do you genuinely feel that if you had this right training in place, the simple nutrition, and accountability from Trevor built around your life, that you would get your goals?" → "100%. 100%."

P11.evidence: Payment collected live and confirmed through the prospect's bank authorisation — "It's all done" / "So it went through." Trevor onboarding booked for 7:15pm on Monday 6 July with receipt of the invite confirmed on the call. The welcome sequence was covered completely: agreement email, Skool community invitation and the onboarding form to complete beforehand, each confirmed. The single deviation is the signature — the script says sign it on the call, the rep deferred it: "just sign the agreement before the meeting with Trevor."

objection_plays.detail: The framing half ran and the diligence half did not, on the one prospect in this batch where the diligence existed to protect. Ran: the upfront norm ("most of the guys just put it up front on a credit card"), the custom-plan line ("we don't have anything like specific payment plans. We do them, but it's always custom, depending on what each individual actually can do"), and the groceries protection line ("last thing Trevor would like from you is to, you know, like get in the program, but not having something to buy groceries"). Did not run: the isolation question, the permission question, and every one of the six financial-picture items — cash on hand, monthly surplus, number of cards, available credit, used versus available, investments. The prospect had already volunteered that he has no job, is spending savings on the restaurant, holds no credit card and is worried about rent. Rather than open that up, the rep messaged a manager and returned with the single most expensive structure available.

The playbook's known clinical gap, and the clearest instance of it in the corpus. The prospect disclosed, unprompted and in detail, a cervical spine injury that left him unable to walk and shifted his neck, a right shoulder he cannot raise with diagnosed arthritis and a cortisone injection into the bursa, ongoing chiropractic treatment, chronic sciatica, chronic severe IBS and fourteen NSAID-induced ulcers. There is no scripted path for this, and the improvisation was to sell. The rep's answer to the clinical picture was programme content — "we need to get this shoulder and movement... Trevor will prepare also short mobility protocols" — and a reassurance framed as shared experience via his own hip story. No question was asked about clearance, restrictions or what his clinicians permit. Contrast with the Nate Slayton call recorded the same day, where the same rep deferred a sale for a pending knee surgery: the difference between the two is judgement, not process, because the process contains nothing at all.

notes: Scored on process this is the rep's strongest call — P4, P5, P6 and P11 are all the best examples in the batch, and the yellow-flag confrontation in the commitment check is worth lifting into training. That makes it the sharpest illustration of what the adherence score cannot see: a well-executed script sold an interest-bearing $7,200 plan to an unemployed man funding a restaurant from savings, and put loaded kettlebell training in front of a cervical spine injury and a shoulder that will not elevate, without one question about medical clearance or one question about his actual finances. The two checks that would have caught both — P2c health conditions and the OC financial picture — are the two he skipped.
